extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and working fiction writers (especially those considering writing a novella); indie/self-published authors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for writing a novella (short longer-than-short-story fiction ~20k–40k words), covering structural, stylistic, and process recommendations specific to the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count / length
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule of thumb puts the novella between 20k and 40k words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this guideline to size your story; the form sits between short story and novel. The author suspects some works near the top end (e.g., Apt Pupil) may be essentially short novels if they exceed ~40k.

rubrics_metrics.name: One plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of the novella dictates that it have one plot. It’s too short to support subplots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can include plot complications, but they should orbit a single story problem. Think of the novella as doing its dance around one problem rather than juggling multiple storylines.

rubrics_metrics.name: One POV
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s almost always best to stick with one point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single POV helps create intimate relationship between Lead character and reader in the short space. Multiple POVs are acceptable only if there is a good, story-driven reason (not to fill pages); example exception: Apt Pupil shifts POV for a narrative reason but may be unusually long.

rubrics_metrics.name: One central question
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one story question per novella, usually in the form: Will X get Y?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate a clear central question (e.g., 'Will Andy Dufresne survive Shawshank?') and make the narrative answer that question. Use examples (Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption; The Old Man and the Sea; A Christmas Carol) to model clarity of central query.

rubrics_metrics.name: One style and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A novella should stick to one tone, one style throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cracking style barriers the way novels sometimes can. Match tone to genre (hard-boiled for pulp, confessional for certain crime novellas, romance/paranormal have their own tones). Maintain consistency to preserve the compact form's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a story idea suited to novella length
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some story ideas that don’t merit 90k words, but may be just right for 30k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick ideas that naturally fit a single-problem, tightly focused treatment—suspense stories are particularly apt. Avoid expansive material that requires many subplots or long worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure your premise is rock solid
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t travel down the road of a flabby idea; come up with a premise that creates the greatest possible stress for the Lead character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test the premise early so you don’t reach ~15k words and discover it isn’t working. Example: One More Lie — man accused of murdering his mistress: innocent of murder but guilty of adultery—creates strong stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in the heat of passion (draft quickly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the story down quickly; novellas can be written fast and require less revision than novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quick drafting (e.g., NaNoWriMo-style burst) to maintain momentum and harness creative energy. The shorter form reduces the need for extensive subplot revision that novels often demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use white space to designate scene changes (avoid chapter markings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of chapters, the novella usually employs white space between scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some writers use numbered sections as a stylistic choice, but avoid labeling sections 'Chapter 1' etc., because chapter labels can interrupt the novella’s flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep escalating stakes — 'How can it get worse?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn up the heat on the character as much as you can; think of the novella as a coil that gets tighter and tighter until you release it at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly ask how the situation can deteriorate to maintain momentum and compression of consequence. Apply this to both internal (character psychology) and external (plot) pressure.
